title: Cognitive Set 07: Meeting Speeds, Quadratics & Logic
description: Features post-meeting travel times, compound doubling, quadratic integer roots, card probability, offer-CTC DI, and verbal reasoning.

questions.question: Two cyclists A and B start at the same moment from towns P and Q toward each other. After crossing each other en route, A takes 4 hours to reach Q and B takes 9 hours to reach P. If A cycles at 18 km/h, what is B's speed?
questions.explanation: By the standard post-meeting theorem, v_A / v_B = sqrt(t_B / t_A) = sqrt(9 / 4) = 3 / 2. Given v_A = 18 km/h, v_B = 18 * (2 / 3) = 12 km/h.
questions.shortcut: v_A / v_B = sqrt(t_B / t_A) = sqrt(9/4) = 3/2 => v_B = 12 km/h.

questions.question: A principal invested at compound interest doubles in 6 years. In how many years from the initial investment will it grow to 16 times its original value at the same annual rate?
questions.explanation: Growth factor 2x occurs every 6 years. Since 16 = 2^4, four doubling intervals are needed: 4 * 6 = 24 years.

questions.question: A canister contains 60 litres of an alcohol-water mixture in the ratio 3 : 2. Fifteen litres of the mixture are drawn out and replaced with 15 litres of pure water. What percentage of the final mixture is alcohol?
questions.explanation: Initial alcohol = (3/5)*60 = 36 L. Removing 15 L (1/4 of mixture) leaves 3/4 of the alcohol: 36 * (3/4) = 27 L. Adding 15 L pure water restores total volume to 60 L. Final alcohol % = (27 / 60) * 100 = 45%.
questions.shortcut: Initial 60% alcohol; removing 1/4 leaves 60% * (3/4) = 45%.

questions.question: How many integer values of x satisfy the inequality x^2 - 5x - 14 < 0?
questions.explanation: Factor the quadratic: (x - 7)(x + 2) < 0, which holds strictly for -2 < x < 7. The integers in this open interval are {-1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, giving 8 integers.
questions.shortcut: Roots are -2 and 7; strict integer count between them = 7 - (-2) - 1 = 8.

questions.question: A circular lawn of radius 20 m is surrounded externally by a uniform 5-metre-wide jogging track. What is the area of the jogging track?
questions.explanation: Outer radius R = 20 + 5 = 25 m; inner radius r = 20 m. Area = pi*(R^2 - r^2) = pi*(625 - 400) = 225*pi sq m.

questions.question: Two cards are drawn simultaneously at random from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that both cards are face cards (Jack, Queen, or King)?
questions.explanation: There are 12 face cards in a 52-card deck (3 per suit * 4 suits). Probability = C(12, 2) / C(52, 2) = (12 * 11) / (52 * 51) = 132 / 2652 = 11 / 221.

questions.question: How many 4-digit numbers strictly greater than 4,000 can be formed using the digits {0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7} without repeating any digit?
questions.explanation: For a 4-digit number > 4,000 using {0,2,3,4,5,7} without repetition, the thousands digit must be 4, 5, or 7 (3 choices). Note 4000 itself is impossible since there is only one 0. Remaining 3 places can be filled from the remaining 5 digits in 5 * 4 * 3 = 60 ways. Total = 3 * 60 = 180.
questions.shortcut: Thousands place: 3 choices {4,5,7}; rest: 5*4*3 = 60 => 180.

questions.question: An intake pump can fill an empty reservoir in 8 hours, but because of a bottom leak it takes 10 hours to fill completely. If the reservoir is full and the pump is turned off, in how many hours will the leak alone empty it?
questions.explanation: Leak rate = 1/8 - 1/10 = (5 - 4) / 40 = 1/40 of the tank per hour. Hence the leak empties the full reservoir in 40 hours.

Five workshops—Java, SQL, Git, Docker, and Spring—are scheduled Monday to Friday (one per day). SQL is immediately after Java. Git is neither on Monday nor on Friday. Docker is two days before Spring (i.e., one workshop sits between Docker and Spring). If Java is on Monday, which workshop is on Wednesday?
questions.explanation: Mon = Java. SQL is immediately after Java => Tue = SQL. Remaining days {Wed, Thu, Fri} hold Git, Docker, Spring. Docker has 1 workshop between it and Spring, so (Docker, Spring) must be (Wed, Fri), forcing Git into Thu (which satisfies Git not on Mon or Fri!). Thus Wednesday = Docker.
questions.shortcut: Mon=Java, Tue=SQL; (Docker, _, Spring) in {Wed, Thu, Fri} forces Wed=Docker, Thu=Git, Fri=Spring.

questions.question: Statements: (1) All caches are in-memory stores. (2) Some in-memory stores are persistent. (3) No persistent store is ephemeral. Conclusions: I. Some caches being persistent is a possibility. II. All in-memory stores being ephemeral is a possibility.
questions.explanation: Since there is no negative constraint between caches and persistent stores, caches can overlap persistent stores (Conclusion I follows). However, since some in-memory stores are persistent and no persistent store is ephemeral, those persistent in-memory stores can NEVER be ephemeral, making Conclusion II impossible.
questions.shortcut: In-memory ∩ Persistent != empty blocks 'All In-memory are Ephemeral'.

questions.question: A is the brother of B. C is the father of A. D is the sister of E. E is the daughter of B. Who is the uncle of D?
questions.explanation: D is the sister of E, and E is B's daughter, so D is also B's child. A is B's brother (male), making A the uncle of B's children (D and E).
questions.shortcut: D & E are B's children; A is B's brother => A is D's uncle.

questions.question: Find the next number in the series: 2, 3, 6, 10, 17, 28, ?
questions.explanation: Each term from the 3rd onward equals the sum of the two preceding terms plus 1: 2+3+1=6, 3+6+1=10, 6+10+1=17, 10+17+1=28, 17+28+1 = 46.

questions.question: In a cipher, SYSTEM is coded as TZTNFU and PYTHON is coded as UZQOPI. How is BINARY coded in the same cipher?
questions.explanation: Split the 6-letter word into two 3-letter halves, reverse each half, and shift every letter +1: SYSTEM -> SYS|TEM -> SYS|MET -> TZT|NFU = TZTNFU. PYTHON -> PYT|HON -> TYP|NOH -> UZQ|OPI = UZQOPI. BINARY -> BIN|ARY -> NIB|YRA -> OJC|ZSB = OJCZSB.
questions.shortcut: Split 3+3 (BIN|ARY), reverse halves (NIB|YRA), add +1 to each letter => OJCZSB.

questions.question: Five distinct positive integers are arranged in strictly increasing order: a < b < c < d < e. What is the median c? Statement I: The average of the five integers is 12, and a + b = 15. Statement II: d + e = 33 and e - d = 3.
options: Both statements I and II together are necessary
questions.explanation: From Statement I: sum = 5*12 = 60, a+b = 15 => c+d+e = 45 (insufficient for c alone). From Statement II: d+e = 33 and e-d = 3 => e = 18, d = 15 (insufficient for c alone). Combining I and II: c = 45 - 33 = 12 (verify order: a+b=15 with a<b<12 works e.g. 7,8,12,15,18). Unique c = 12!
questions.shortcut: I gives c+d+e=45; II gives d+e=33 => together c = 12.

questions.question: A rearrangement engine processes the array [54, 19, 82, 37, 61] as follows: in odd-numbered steps (Step 1, 3, ...), it moves the smallest remaining unsorted element to the leftmost unsorted slot; in even-numbered steps (Step 2, 4, ...), it moves the largest remaining unsorted element to the rightmost unsorted slot. What is the 3rd number from the left after Step 2?
questions.explanation: Input: [54, 19, 82, 37, 61]. Step 1 (smallest 19 to left): [19, 54, 82, 37, 61]. Step 2 (largest 82 of remaining [54, 82, 37, 61] to right): [19, 54, 37, 61, 82]. The 3rd number from the left is 37.
questions.shortcut: Step 1 pulls 19 to front => [19, 54, 82, 37, 61]; Step 2 pushes 82 to back => [19, 54, 37, 61, 82].

questions.question: If '+' means division, '-' means multiplication, '*' means subtraction, and '/' means addition, then evaluate: 24 + 6 - 5 / 12 * 8
questions.explanation: Substitute operators carefully and apply BODMAS: 24 / 6 * 5 + 12 - 8 = 4 * 5 + 12 - 8 = 20 + 12 - 8 = 24.

questions.question: Rule: 'If a pull request modifies a database migration script, it requires approval from a DBA.' Which statement is logically equivalent to this rule?
options: If a pull request has DBA approval, it must modify a database migration script
If a pull request does not modify a database migration script, it does not require DBA approval
If a pull request does not have DBA approval, it cannot legitimately modify a database migration script
Only database migration scripts ever require DBA approval
questions.explanation: The statement 'If P then Q' (P -> Q) is logically equivalent only to its contrapositive 'If not Q then not P'. Here: if it lacks DBA approval (not Q), it does not/cannot validly modify a migration script (not P).
questions.shortcut: P -> Q is strictly equivalent to (~Q -> ~P).

questions.question:
In a 3x3 grid, each row follows the same arithmetic rule:
Row 1: [6, 9, 45]
Row 2: [8, 5, 39]
Row 3: [7, 11, ?]
Find the missing value.
questions.explanation: Rule: Third column = (First column + Second column) * 3. Row 1: (6 + 9) * 3 = 45. Row 2: (8 + 5) * 3 = 39. Row 3: (7 + 11) * 3 = 18 * 3 = 54.
questions.shortcut: Add the first two numbers in each row and multiply by 3: (7 + 11) * 3 = 54.

questions.passage: When organizations migrate from synchronous REST chains to event-driven message brokers, they gain temporal decoupling: an order service can emit an 'OrderPlaced' event without waiting for email, loyalty, and warehouse consumers to respond. Yet asynchronous messaging trades immediate consistency for eventual consistency. Without dead-letter queues, idempotent consumers, and schema registries, transient payload mismatches silently stall downstream pipelines—turning what looked like clean decoupling into invisible data drift.
questions.question: What is the author's central point about event-driven architectures?
options: Synchronous REST chains always scale better than message brokers
Asynchronous decoupling brings eventual-consistency risks that require safeguards like dead-letter queues and schema registries
Order services should wait for email consumers before confirming checkouts
Event-driven pipelines eliminate all data drift automatically
questions.explanation: The passage balances the benefit (temporal decoupling) against the hidden risks (eventual consistency, silent stalls/drift) unless safeguards (DLQs, idempotency, schema registries) are used.
questions.shortcut: Combine the 'gain' in sentence 1 with the 'Yet... Without...' warning in sentences 2–3.

Yet asynchronous messaging trades immediate consistency for eventual consistency. questions.question: In the passage, 'temporal decoupling' refers to the ability of a producer service to:
options: Delete historical events on a fixed schedule
Publish an event without blocking on downstream consumers to finish processing
Run synchronous database transactions across multiple regions
Bypass schema validation during peak holiday traffic
questions.explanation: Directly after the colon, temporal decoupling is explained as emitting an 'OrderPlaced' event without waiting for email, loyalty, and warehouse consumers to respond.
questions.shortcut: Read the definition right after 'temporal decoupling:'.

questions.question: Find the erroneous segment: 'The release lead remarked that (A) / if the staging cluster was (B) / configured identically to production, (C) / the SSL bug would have surfaced earlier. (D)'
questions.explanation: The main clause uses 'would have surfaced' (third conditional counterfactual), so the 'if' clause requires past perfect 'had been configured' (or at minimum subjunctive 'were', never indicative 'was').
questions.shortcut: Counterfactual 'if' + 'would have surfaced' requires 'had been', not 'was'.

questions.question:
Arrange P, Q, R, S into a coherent paragraph:
P. This illusion breaks down when two concurrent threads read the same balance, compute updates locally, and overwrite each other.
Q. Optimistic locking resolves such lost updates by attaching a version column to every row.
R. Developers working solely with single-user local tests rarely notice race conditions in read-modify-write flows.
S. If the row's version changed between read and commit, the database rejects the stale write so the application can safely retry.
questions.explanation: R states why developers miss race conditions locally. P explains how 'This illusion' fails under concurrency. Q introduces optimistic locking to solve 'such lost updates'. S details how the version check works. Order: R-P-Q-S.
questions.shortcut: R (local illusion) -> P ('This illusion' + overwrite) -> Q ('such lost updates') -> S (version mechanism).

questions.question: Choose the accurate phrase: 'All graduating trainees must comply [with] the client's data-privacy charter.'
questions.explanation: The verb 'comply' always pairs with 'with' ('comply with'), whereas 'adhere' pairs with 'to'.
questions.shortcut: 'Comply with' vs 'adhere to'.

questions.question: Complete the sentence: 'Early rumors of a hiring freeze proved ______, as the campus division actually ______ its intake by twenty percent.'
questions.explanation: Because the division actually increased ('expanded') hiring by 20%, rumors of a freeze were false or baseless ('unfounded').
questions.shortcut: 'actually +20%' contradicts freeze => rumors were 'unfounded'.

questions.question: Spot the grammatical error: 'Hardly had the monitor flagged high heap usage (A) / when the JVM triggered a full GC pause (B) / and drops incoming connections (C) / for twelve seconds. (D)'
questions.explanation: The sentence narrates a past event ('had flagged', 'triggered'), so the parallel verb in segment (C) must be past tense 'dropped', not present 'drops'.
questions.shortcut: Parallel past verbs: 'triggered ... and dropped'.

questions.question:
Order P, Q, R, S logically:
P. Instead of blocking the caller while generating a heavy PDF report, the API returns HTTP 202 Accepted with a job ID.
Q. Synchronous HTTP handlers time out cleanly at thirty seconds under most reverse proxies.
R. The client then polls a lightweight status endpoint until the background worker marks the artifact ready.
S. Long-running export tasks must therefore shift to an asynchronous job pattern.
questions.explanation: Q states the 30-second proxy timeout limit. S draws the implication ('therefore shift to async job pattern'). P explains how the API responds immediately (HTTP 202). R completes the workflow ('then polls'). Order: Q-S-P-R.
questions.shortcut: Constraint (Q) -> 'therefore' async pattern (S) -> HTTP 202 (P) -> 'then polls' (R).

questions.question: Pick the correct improvement: 'The new search index is [more faster] than the legacy full-scan filter.'
questions.explanation: Never combine 'more' with an '-er' comparative ('more faster'). Use an intensifier such as 'much faster' or 'far faster'.
questions.shortcut: Avoid double comparatives ('more faster' -> 'much faster').

questions.question: Hypothesis: 'Introducing mandatory peer code reviews reduced post-release production bugs at FinCore by 30%.' Which piece of evidence most STRENGTHENS this hypothesis?
options: FinCore also upgraded its office Wi-Fi routers during the same year
In a sister division at FinCore with identical tech stack and release cadence that did NOT adopt peer reviews, bug rates stayed flat
Junior developers reported spending more time reading pull requests
FinCore's customer base grew by 12% over the year
questions.explanation: A matched control group (sister division with identical stack/cadence without peer reviews showing flat bug rates) isolates peer reviews as the causal driver.
questions.shortcut: Controlled comparison showing unchanged bugs where peer reviews were absent strongly confirms causality.
